events.title: The martyrdom of Pope St. Sixtus II
events.shortBlurb: A pope was cut down with his deacons at the altar in the Roman catacombs under the persecution of Valerian…
body: Early in August 258 the Emperor Valerian sharpened the persecution with a second edict: a year after forbidding Christians to gather in the cemeteries, he now ordered bishops, priests, and deacons put to death at once. The blow fell first on Rome, where Sixtus II had sat as pope for a year, having succeeded Stephen I in August 257.

On 6 August, as Sixtus sat teaching the brethren in a catacomb on the Appian Way, soldiers seized him and beheaded him. Four of his seven deacons died with him, as Cyprian of Carthage wrote in a letter; two more, Felicissimus and Agapitus, suffered the same day and were laid in the cemetery of Praetextatus. The pope's body was laid in the papal crypt of the cemetery of Callixtus.

Four days later, on 10 August, his archdeacon Lawrence followed him to death; that same autumn Cyprian himself was martyred at Carthage. Rome kept the memory green: Sixtus was named in the canon of the Roman Mass among the first martyrs after the apostles, Pope Damasus adorned his tomb with verses, and his feast on 6 August appears already in the fourth-century calendar.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Paul VI
events.shortBlurb: The pope who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close died on the feast of the Transfiguration…
body: Giovanni Battista Montini was born on 26 September 1897 at Concesio, near Brescia. Ordained in 1920, he served more than thirty years in the Secretariat of State under Pius XI and Pius XII, then governed Milan as archbishop from 1954, until his election as pope on 21 June 1963, taking the name Paul VI.

He reconvened the Second Vatican Council after John XXIII's death and closed it on 8 December 1965, then bore the weight of its reception: the revised Roman Missal and the reform of the curia. He was the first pope to travel by air, journeying to the Holy Land in 1964, to the United Nations in 1965 to plead 'no more war', and in all to six continents.

His encyclicals included Populorum progressio on the development of peoples (1967) and Humanae vitae on the transmission of life (1968), the latter answered by dissent. Worn by grief at the murder of his friend Aldo Moro that May, he died of a heart attack at Castel Gandolfo on the evening of 6 August 1978, the feast of the Transfiguration; he was canonized by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018.
